documents.title: GraphRAG architecture
documents.text: GraphRAG builds an entity graph from source documents. Community detection groups related entities and creates summaries. At query time it retrieves graph neighborhoods and community reports, then assembles evidence for a question. The graph can connect facts scattered across several pages. Global questions can use hierarchical community summaries. Local questions can traverse entity relationships. The graph construction adds indexing cost and can introduce extraction errors. A conventional vector RAG system instead embeds passages and retrieves nearby vectors without explicit entity edges. GraphRAG is useful when relationships and corpus-wide themes matter, while its extra indexing cost may not help every question.

documents.title: Dense vector retrieval
documents.text: A dense retrieval system maps passages and questions to embedding vectors. A similarity index ranks passages by cosine proximity to the query vector. Semantic retrieval may find a paraphrase even when the query and passage share few surface words. Dense vectors can miss exact identifiers and rare technical strings. The encoder model and its dimension must be recorded with the index. Changing embedding models usually requires rebuilding vectors. Candidate retrieval can be followed by a cross encoder that compares each question and passage together.

documents.title: BM25 lexical search
documents.text: BM25 ranks documents by term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalization. It is strong for exact names, rare identifiers, acronyms and technical terms such as BGE-M3 or GPT-5. SQLite FTS5 exposes bm25 scores where lower numerical values rank first. A search application must escape arbitrary user text before sending it to MATCH. BM25 does not understand paraphrases unless query expansion is added. This makes it complementary to dense vector retrieval. Reciprocal rank fusion combines rank positions from both lists without treating their raw scores as comparable.

documents.title: RAG retrieval evaluation
documents.text: Retrieval evaluation uses labeled relevant passages or documents for each question. Recall at K measures how many known relevant items appear in the first K results. Precision at K measures the relevant fraction of K returned items. Mean reciprocal rank rewards placing the first relevant item near the top. Normalized discounted cumulative gain supports graded relevance labels. A useful benchmark includes paraphrases, exact strings, distractors and highly similar irrelevant evidence. Report latency and index size alongside ranking quality. A small fixture supports regression testing but cannot establish performance on every topic.

documents.title: Evidence grounded answer quality
documents.text: A grounded answer should cite source passages that support each important claim. Hallucination occurs when an answer asserts unsupported facts or misrepresents the cited evidence. Retrieval recall is a prerequisite for answer grounding: if the relevant passage is absent, the generation stage cannot cite it. A faithfulness check compares claims against retrieved evidence. Citation accuracy checks whether the cited passage actually entails a claim. An abstention policy can prevent unsupported answers when evidence is weak. These are answer evaluation methods, separate from retrieval ranking metrics.

documents.title: Retrieval latency engineering
documents.text: Interactive retrieval latency includes query embedding time, vector search time, lexical search time, fusion time and cross encoder reranking time. Reranking many passages can dominate CPU response time. A two stage design first retrieves a bounded candidate set, then reranks only those candidates. Batching pairs reduces overhead but can increase memory consumption. Report p50 and p95 across representative queries. Cache models across requests, and avoid loading the encoder for every query. Index construction time and query response time measure different costs.

documents.title: Graph database administration
documents.text: A graph database stores nodes and edges and supports traversals. Indexes may accelerate graph queries. Database administrators monitor storage, backups and query latency. Community detection can be run as an analytics workload. These database operations do not by themselves define GraphRAG retrieval or evidence generation. An entity graph is only one component of a research pipeline. This passage shares graph terminology with GraphRAG but addresses database administration instead of retrieval architecture.

documents.title: Search engine benchmarking
documents.text: Search engine benchmarks often compare ranking methods and response latency. A benchmark might measure precision, recall, query throughput and memory use. These terms overlap with RAG retrieval evaluation, but a throughput experiment with no relevance judgments cannot measure nDCG or MRR. Hardware and caching affect latency. Always separate the measured workload from conclusions about answer quality. An efficient search engine can still return irrelevant evidence.
